```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

T = Path("../results/tables")
S = json.loads((T / "site_settings.json").read_text("utf-8"))
CAL = {row["id"]: row for row in json.loads((T / "rollout_calendar.json").read_text("utf-8"))["items"]}
reg = pd.read_csv(T / "run1" / "registered_tests.csv")
n_tests = len(reg)
n_sig = int((reg["significant"] == True).sum())
n_regions = len(S["regions"])
n_fire_years = int(reg[(reg["test"] == "H3a") & (reg["region"] == "PNW")]["n"].iloc[0])
NEXT = next(row for row in CAL.values() if row["reader"] and not row["done"])
```

## Overview

I asked whether the winter before a fire season says how much will burn, and
whether El Niño is the useful part of that winter. I fixed
`{python} n_tests` tests in writing on `{python} CAL["plan_frozen"]["when"]`,
before opening any fire data, and ran them once. `{python} n_sig` are
significant after correcting for the number of tests, and none of those links
El Niño itself to burned area. A forecast for `{python} S["forecast_year"]`
goes up before the season and is checked against it afterwards.

::::: {.overview .column-body-outset}
:::: {}
<p class="ov">Data areas</p>

- <i class="sw fire"></i>**Burned area.** Hectares burned each fire season by
  fires of `{python} S["min_fire_ha"]` ha or more, from `{python} S["fire_first_year"]`.
- <i class="sw water"></i>**Winter rain.** December to February and October
  to March precipitation, from `{python} S["climate_first_year"] + 1`.
- <i class="sw snow"></i>**Snowpack.** Snow on the ground on 1 April, with
  snow stations as a check.
- <i class="sw temp"></i>**Temperature.** Summer and spring means, and a
  drought index that combines temperature with precipitation.
- <i class="sw enso"></i>**El Niño.** NOAA's `{python} S["enso_index"]` for
  each winter.
::::

:::: {}
<p class="ov">Regions covered</p>

- **North:** Pacific Northwest (Washington, Oregon, Idaho), British Columbia,
  Alberta.
- **Far north:** Alaska, Yukon.
- **California:** split at `{python} S["ca_split_lat"]`°N into Northern and
  Southern.
- `{python} n_regions` regions in all, each a whole state, province or
  territory.
::::

:::: {}
<p class="ov">Hypotheses and why</p>

- **Two routes.** In the north an El Niño winter runs warm and dry, so less
  snow and an earlier fire season. In Southern California it runs wet, so
  more grass to burn.
- **Tested in pieces.** El Niño to winter weather, winter weather to burned
  area, and El Niño to burned area directly.
- **Fixed first.** With about `{python} n_fire_years` seasons a record can be
  made to say almost anything, so the tests were written down before the
  fire data was opened.
::::
:::::

## Two pathways from one El Niño

<!-- Two layouts of one diagram: the wide one from 576 px up, the narrow one
     below (Bootstrap classes d-none d-sm-block / d-sm-none). Read from
     results/ at render time; Quarto copies the outputs into _site/. -->

:::: {.d-none .d-sm-block}
::: {.fig-light}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Flow diagram. El Niño, warm water in the central-eastern tropical Pacific, makes the Pacific jet stream extend east and shift south. North pathway (PNW, BC, AB): a milder, often drier winter, then less snow and earlier melt, then an earlier or longer fire season. South pathway (SoCal): a wetter winter, then more grass growth, then more fine fuel once the grass cures and larger grass fires. Footnote: these are expected pathways tested in this study; AK and YT are also analysed, as northern regions, with no pathway drawn because their hypotheses are not yet set; NorCal is also analysed, as a contrast region, with no pathway drawn because its expected response is not yet set."
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(filename="../results/figures/mechanism.svg")
```
:::
